messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Architect
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Violence: Violence, Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled
  Memory: Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marcus is a 49-year-old architect, married, who presented for his initial assessment carrying the particular stillness of a man who has spent months trying not to draw attention to himself. He was referred following a significant decline in his occupational functioning and a recent disclosure to his wife that he had not slept more than a few consecutive hours in over a year. His PCL-5 score of 52 places him firmly in the severe range, and the picture that emerged across the first two sessions was one of a man whose inner world had been fundamentally reorganised by something he saw — not something that happened to him, a distinction he returns to with something close to shame.

Fourteen months ago, Marcus was on a site visit to a mixed-use development project in a neighbourhood undergoing rapid redevelopment. He was walking through a partially completed ground-floor corridor when he witnessed a violent assault — a sustained, close-range attack on a man he did not know, carried out by two others. The smell of the space — concrete dust, something metallic, a sharp chemical note from nearby adhesive work — saturated the experience. He was close enough to feel nauseous, close enough that the details became involuntary and total. He did not intervene. He pressed himself against the wall and watched until the assailants left, and by the time he reached for his phone his hands were shaking badly enough that he misdialled twice.

In the weeks that followed, the memory refused to settle into the past. Marcus found he could not reconstruct the event in any reliable sequence — he could not say with confidence what happened first, what happened after — and when he tried to describe it to the police or later to his wife, the words simply were not there. He knew what he had witnessed; he could not render it in language. This fragmentation meant that when memories surfaced they did not arrive as recollections but as re-immersions: the smell of adhesive on a job site, or the particular quality of nausea he had felt, could collapse the distance between then and now entirely, so that he was not remembering the corridor but back inside it. These sensory triggers — a related smell, a wave of nausea, anything that carried even a distant echo of violence — became the fault lines of his daily life, and each time one activated, the fragmented memory surged forward with it, uncontrolled and present-tense.

The nature of that memory — its unprocessed, here-and-now quality — fed directly into a state of near-constant threat perception. Marcus had come to understand the world as a place in which violence could arrive without warning in any enclosed space, and his nervous system appeared to have accepted this as operational fact. He began positioning himself with his back to the wall in every room he entered — a habit that had become automatic — and scanning for exits the moment he crossed any threshold. His work as an architect now placed him daily in the very environments that most activated this vigilance: building sites, open-plan offices, client presentation rooms, corridors under construction. What had once been his professional domain had become a landscape of threat assessments. He was jumpy in ways his junior colleagues had begun to notice, flinching at unexpected sounds, and this hypervigilance in turn kept him in a state of perpetual readiness that made the next trigger easier to find and harder to dismiss. The threat he perceived in any given room sharpened his attention to exactly the sensory details — smells, sounds, physical sensations — most likely to return him to the assault, and the assault, once activated, confirmed that the threat had been real all along.

Beneath all of this ran a current of belief that Marcus found most difficult to articulate. He had come to feel, in a way he recognised as irrational but could not dislodge, that something intrinsic to him had made the event happen — that a person without his particular flaw would not have been there, would not have frozen, would not have watched. He felt isolated from colleagues and from his wife in a way that had become structural rather than situational, certain that what he carried could not be shared or understood. These appraisals of fundamental fault and helplessness intensified his sense of ongoing danger, as though his own nature marked him as a target, and they lowered the threshold at which ordinary sensory experience became threatening. It was his wife who finally insisted he seek help, after finding him one evening standing in their kitchen with his back against the far wall, scanning the room. What Marcus most fears is that the man he was before that corridor no longer exists. What he most hopes is that someone will tell him he is wrong.
